steps.title: A function calling itself
steps.content: Recursion solves a problem by reducing it to a smaller version of the same problem. Every correct recursive function needs a base case that stops the calls.
steps.tip: Find the base case before tracing the recursive call.

steps.title: Identify the base case
steps.prompt: For factorial(n), which is a valid base case?
steps.explanation: 0! = 1. Returning 1 at n==0 allows all recursive calls to unwind.

steps.title: Trace the call stack
steps.content: Each recursive call gets its own local variables and waits for the smaller call to return. After the base case, results combine while the stack unwinds.

steps.title: Count recursive calls
steps.prompt: A function calls itself with n−1 until n==0. Starting at n=4, how many calls are made including the base call?

steps.title: Avoid infinite recursion
steps.content: Each recursive call should move toward the base case. If the input does not get closer to the stopping condition, recursion may never end and can overflow the call stack.
steps.example: For n>0, call f(n−1). Calling f(n) again makes no progress.

questions.prompt: What must a recursive function have?
questions.explanation: The base case stops further recursive calls.

questions.prompt: What happens as recursive calls return?
questions.explanation: Calls return in reverse order, unwinding the call stack.

questions.prompt: If f(n) calls f(n−1), which input moves toward base case n=0?
questions.explanation: Subtracting one moves a positive n closer to zero.

questions.prompt: What can happen if recursion never reaches a base case?
questions.explanation: Unbounded recursive calls can exhaust the call stack.
